stimulus: Magnets remember, supposedly, but the first oddity is that a piece of iron has no brain and no clock, only a history written into where its domain walls got stuck. Physicists draw the hysteresis loop, that fat lopsided oval, and read memory off the gap between going up and coming down. But a gap alone could be slow relaxation, so they wait, and wait, and watch remanence decay logarithmically, which is a clue that there are many barriers, not one. Then the wiping tricks: demagnetize with a shrinking AC field and the loop's memory spirals to nothing, like erasing a chalkboard with gentler and gentler strokes. Oddly the reverse is also true, since first-order reversal curves let you read out the whole distribution of tiny switching units, a fossil census. Paleomagnetists lean on this, reading ancient lava as a compass frozen at cooling time, though a later lightning strike can overwrite it, so they heat in steps to peel layers back like onion skin. Return-point memory sounds like a fairy tale: cycle partway, come back, and the system retraces exactly. Shape-memory alloys and crumpled paper do something similar, and Preisach models treat the whole thing as a crowd of little switches with two thresholds each. Is the memory in the switches or in their coupling? Spin glasses ask that too, with their aging and rejuvenation, temperature dips remembered like stubborn grudges.

Research question: "What analyses or measurements would best test whether AP-1 acts as a cellular memory mechanism?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

ideas.title: Hysteresis loop of AP-1 dose-response
ideas.description: Ramp a stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or PMA/ERK input driving FOS/JUN) up and then down in single cells, and measure AP-1 activity and target-gene output (live reporters, chromatin accessibility) to see if the descending branch differs from the ascending one. A gap that persists after long waits, and decays logarithmically rather than exponentially, would indicate stable memory with many barriers rather than slow relaxation.

ideas.title: Remanence decay and erasure by decaying pulses
ideas.description: After a transient stimulus, track AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN), accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target expression over days to weeks to get the decay kinetics. Then try to erase the memory with a shrinking-amplitude oscillating stimulus (analogous to AC demagnetization) or by acute degron removal of AP-1, to test whether AP-1 is needed for maintenance rather than only for initiation.

ideas.title: First-order reversal curve census of AP-1 sites
ideas.description: Apply stimulus histories with different peak and reversal levels, then read out accessibility or reporter activity at individual AP-1 enhancers. Fit a Preisach-style model with two thresholds per site to get the distribution of switching thresholds, and test return-point memory: cycle partway, return, and check whether the state is retraced exactly. This shows whether memory lives in independent enhancer switches or in their coupling.

ideas.title: Stepwise peeling of layered memory by order-of-exposure experiments
ideas.description: Expose cells to sequential stimuli (e.g., wounding, then inflammation, then a third signal) in different orders. Use time-resolved ATAC/CUT&Tag to see whether later AP-1 events overwrite or add to earlier accessible sites, and use stepwise degron depletion to peel back the layers. This tells you whether the memory is hierarchical and which earlier imprints a later stimulus can overwrite.

ideas.title: Switch versus coupling test via perturbation of cooperativity
ideas.description: Separate the contribution of individual AP-1 motifs from that of the surrounding network (positive feedback of FOS/JUN on its own promoters, pioneer cooperation with partner factors like ETS or the SWI/SNF complex). Mutate motifs at single enhancers by CRISPR, and block feedback loops or chromatin remodelers, then measure single-cell bistability and the persistence of the primed state. If memory is lost when coupling is cut but not when motifs are retained, it is a network property rather than a property of the individual sites.
